metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
In AI data center retrofits, the floor is often the binding constraint before the power is: liquid-cooled racks are heavy enough that structural limits arrive ahead of electrical ones.

The weight comes from what liquid cooling adds. Coolant, manifolds, and batteries sit on top of the rack itself, and a rack built for that load is dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered around. Floor loading limits measure the structural weight a raised floor or slab supports per square foot against the actual weight of what is installed on it. That is a property of the building, not of the equipment.

This matters for AI because it reorders the retrofit problem. Electrical capacity is the constraint the industry watches, and it is the one that gets planned for. Structure is harder to change than a service upgrade, and it is reached sooner than expected. A site can have power available and still not be able to hold the racks that would use it.

What the data does not cover is scale. There is no threshold, no count of affected sites, no cost, and no timeline. It states that structural limits are hit before electrical ones more often than expected, without saying how often or where. The two related metrics, server utilization rate and stranded power and space per cabinet, sit in the same capacity category, but nothing here ties floor loading to either of them.
